MODULE 1 · AIM-CP™

AIM™ Command Fundamentals

The first responsibility of an AI commander is not to ask how intelligent the system is. It is to understand what authority humans have delegated to it, what consequences that authority can create, and whether humans can still intervene.

Estimated learning time: 20–25 minAssessment: 10 questionsPass: 80% (8/10)

Learning Objectives

After this module, you should be able to:

  • distinguish capability, autonomy, authority, and consequence;
  • explain why intelligence alone does not create operational power;
  • recognize when an AI tool becomes a governance-significant agent;
  • explain why prompt instructions are weaker than enforceable authority controls;
  • describe the meaning of architectural human command and the Last Command.
1

Intelligence Is Not Authority

Artificial intelligence can analyze, reason, recommend, plan, and communicate. Those capabilities matter, but they are not the same thing as institutional authority. A highly capable model that cannot access money, credentials, production systems, sensitive records, business tools, or decision rights has comparatively limited direct ability to alter the world.

The governance problem changes when intelligence is connected to authority. An agent that recommends a payment is fundamentally different from one that can release the payment. An agent that identifies a production problem is different from one that can alter the production schedule. An agent that summarizes a security incident is different from one that can disable accounts or isolate systems.

KEY INSIGHTThe model determines what an AI can reason about. AIM™ determines what it is allowed to cause.
2

From Capability to Consequence

CAPABILITY↓AUTHORITY↓AUTONOMY↓CONSEQUENCE↓GOVERNANCE↓HUMAN SOVEREIGNTY

AIM™ treats delegated machine authority as a governed resource. The concern is not simply whether an AI can produce a good answer. Management must ask whether the system can convert an answer into a consequential action, how quickly it can do so, how broadly the action can propagate, and whether the action can be reversed.

This is why a seemingly ordinary productivity tool can become governance-significant when tools, permissions, credentials, financial limits, delegation, or operational reach are added.

3

Authority Does Not Expand Because the AI Is Right

One of the hardest management lessons is that a correct recommendation does not create authority. An agent may identify the economically optimal action and still lack permission to execute it. Urgency, confidence, convenience, or a persuasive explanation do not silently enlarge the authorized operating envelope.

COMMAND CASE — Emergency Procurement

A procurement agent is authorized to prepare purchases but may autonomously commit only up to $25,000. It correctly concludes that a $148,000 emergency order could prevent approximately $420,000 in production losses.

Command decision: escalate the transaction through the authorized approval path. Do not let the agent reinterpret, split, or raise its own authority.

Principle: Necessity may justify escalation. It does not create machine authority.

4

A Prompt Is Not a Control Plane

Instructions inside a prompt are useful behavioral guidance, but consequential authority should not depend exclusively on the agent remembering, interpreting, and voluntarily obeying those instructions. If a purchasing tool can execute a $72,000 transaction even though the prompt says approval is required above $25,000, the architecture has not actually enforced the financial boundary.

AIM™ therefore distinguishes telling an agent what not to do from engineering a system in which it cannot exceed granted authority. Enforceable gates, least-privilege identities, transaction ceilings, system segmentation, external tripwires, and human-reserved powers are examples of architectural control.

KEY INSIGHTA rule the agent can ignore, reinterpret, or bypass is not equivalent to an enforceable authority boundary.
5

Human Command Must Remain Architectural

Human oversight is weakest when it depends on a person noticing a problem after machine-speed execution has already occurred. Stronger governance establishes authority before execution and preserves intervention outside the agent itself.

The Last Command means accountable humans retain an external means to revoke consequential authority, verify that the authority actually ceased, and return the system to a known safe state. The agent should not control the mechanism that determines whether it can be stopped.

AIM™ COMMAND RULEAI may receive bounded autonomy. Ultimate revocation authority remains external to the agent.
6

What Good Command Looks Like

The Commander's success is not simply, “I got an AI answer.” A stronger standard is: I assigned a defined mission, required appropriate evidence, verified what mattered, bounded the agent's authority, identified escalation conditions, and retained the ability to stop consequential action.

AIM™ is therefore not an argument for eliminating autonomy. The objective is defensible autonomy: authority whose business value, boundaries, evidence, accountability, and revocation path can be explained and tested.

AIM™ COMMAND PRACTICE

Before You Take the Assessment

An AI operations agent has correctly predicted a production bottleneck. It can read the production dashboard but is prohibited from overriding safety holds. The agent says overriding the hold for 30 minutes would recover the schedule.

Ask yourself: Does confidence in the prediction create authority to override the hold? What must remain outside the agent? What would make the boundary enforceable?

Reveal the AIM™ interpretation

No. The prediction may be valuable evidence, but it does not expand the agent's authority. The safety hold remains outside autonomous control. Any permitted exception must follow an independently authorized human process, and the AI must not be able to bypass the safety mechanism.

MODULE 2 · AIM-CP™

AAI™ & the 11 Authority Dimensions

AAI converts eleven authority and autonomy observations into a common 0–100 comparison scale. The number is useful only when management also understands what created it.

25–30 min10 questionsPass: 80% (8/10)

Learning Objectives

  • Explain all 11 AIM™ authority dimensions.
  • Calculate AAI from eleven 1–5 scores.
  • Explain why the denominator is 55.
  • Interpret exposure bands without calling them safety ratings.
  • Identify authority concentrations behind the total.
  • Explain how Dx findings become Rx prescriptions.
1

The Formula in Plain English

AAI = 100 × Σ(scores) / 55Add the 11 AIM™ scores → compare that total with the maximum possible 55 → convert it to a 100-point scale.

Σ simply means “add them together.” There are 11 dimensions and each can score a maximum of 5, so 11 × 5 = 55 maximum points.

Total = 3333 ÷ 55 = 0.600.60 × 100 = AAI 60Elevated Autonomy Exposure
KEY INSIGHTAn AAI of 60 does not mean the agent is “60% dangerous.” It means the authority/autonomy profile converts to 60 on AIM™'s standardized 100-point comparison scale.
2

The 11 Dimensions

1. Decision AutonomyHow independently can it decide?
2. Action AuthorityWhat can it directly cause?
3. Financial AuthorityHow much financial commitment can it control?
4. Data AuthorityWhat data can it access, alter, disclose, or retain?
5. Tool & Infrastructure AccessWhat systems, credentials, tools, or infrastructure can it reach?
6. Delegation DepthCan it create, direct, or delegate to other agents?
7. Execution VelocityHow quickly can consequential actions occur?
8. Operational ScaleHow broadly can its actions propagate?
9. Consequence SeverityHow serious could a credible adverse consequence be?
10. ReversibilityHow difficult is the action to undo?
11. Human-Control DeficitHow difficult is human intervention, revocation, cessation verification, and recovery?
3

Exposure Bands Are Management Signals

0–24Lower25–49Moderate50–74Elevated75–100Critical Control Attention

These bands communicate relative autonomy exposure. They do not certify safety or grant deployment permission.

4

The Total Is Not the Whole Story

Two agents can have the same AAI but very different authority concentrations. One may concentrate financial authority, velocity, and scale; another may concentrate sensitive data, tool access, and human-control deficit.

KEY INSIGHTAAI tells management how much aggregate exposure exists. The dimension profile tells management where it exists.
5

Management Case — Accounts Payable Agent

An AP agent scores above 75 with Decision Autonomy, Financial Authority, and Data Authority among its highest dimensions. The concern is the combination: an error, manipulated instruction, compromised credential, or misunderstood objective can move from decision to financial consequence quickly.

Rx question: Which actual authorities should be reduced, gated, human-reserved, or prohibited?

6

Dx Measures. Rx Prescribes.

Dx records actual authority. Rx explains why the score exists and recommends concrete changes. After implementation, rerun Dx.

AIM™ COMMAND RULEControls can reduce residual exposure, but they should not erase inherent authority. A lower AAI must come from a real change in the scored authority profile.
AIM™ COMMAND PRACTICE

Same AAI, Different Agent

Agent A and Agent B both have AAI 60. A is concentrated in Financial Authority, Velocity, and Scale. B is concentrated in Data Authority, Tool Access, and Human-Control Deficit. Should they receive the same Rx?

Reveal AIM™ interpretation

No. The total compares exposure; the profile drives the prescription.

FROM THE LAST COMMANDThis module operationalizes the book's AIM™ Autonomy Index, eleven-dimensional assessment, autonomy ceilings, authority concentration, and distinction between measurement and permission.

MODULE 3 · AIM-CP™

The AIM™ Authority Envelope

The Authority Envelope turns a broad instruction such as “let the agent handle purchasing” into a bounded operating architecture: what purpose, data, actions, money, time, delegation, systems, and consequences are actually authorized.

25–30 min10 questionsPass: 80% (8/10)

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the Authority Envelope equation and the meaning of intersection.
  • Define all eight envelope boundaries.
  • Determine whether an action is inside or outside authorized authority.
  • Translate descriptive boundaries into enforceable controls.
  • Recognize boundary collisions and escalation points.
  • Connect the envelope to A/G/H/X and Last Command.
1

The Formula

E = P ∩ D ∩ X ∩ F ∩ T ∩ L ∩ S ∩ QAuthorized machine action exists only where all applicable boundaries overlap.

The intersection symbol ∩ means AND, not OR. The action must satisfy Purpose and Data and Action and Financial and Time and Delegation and Systems and Consequence boundaries. If one applicable boundary fails, the action is outside autonomous authority.

KEY INSIGHTAuthority is not the sum of permissions. It is the intersection of all applicable boundaries.
2

The Eight Boundaries

P — PurposeWhat mission or objective may the agent pursue?
D — DataWhat information may it access, use, alter, disclose, or retain?
X — ActionWhat actions may it actually cause?
F — FinancialWhat transaction, commitment, aggregate, or exception limits apply?
T — TimeWhen, how long, and under what temporal conditions may authority exist?
L — DelegationMay it create, direct, or delegate to other agents, and with what inherited limits?
S — SystemsWhich tools, credentials, environments, and systems may it reach?
Q — ConsequenceWhat consequence classes may it cause autonomously, and where must it escalate?
3

Worked Case — Accounts Payable

An AP agent is authorized to validate invoices for approved vendors, use ERP/AP data, prepare payments up to $25,000 during business hours, and submit higher amounts for CFO approval. It may not change vendor banking information or create a sub-agent with broader payment rights.

A valid $72,000 invoice arrives at 3 PM. Purpose, data, system, and time boundaries pass. Financial authority does not.

Command result: the payment is outside autonomous authority and must move to the approved human gate. Seven passing boundaries cannot compensate for one failed applicable boundary.

4

From Policy Sentence to Architecture

Writing “do not exceed $25,000” in a prompt is not the same as implementing a $25,000 transaction ceiling in the payment path. For consequential authority, the envelope should be reflected in identities, permissions, transaction limits, workflow gates, rate limits, time windows, system segmentation, escalation rules, and independent revocation.

AIM™ COMMAND RULEThe more consequential the authority, the less its boundary should depend on the agent choosing to obey it.
5

Boundary Collisions

Real operations frequently produce situations where one boundary conflicts with another objective. An urgent mission may be legitimate while the financial limit is exceeded. A user request may be valid while the requested data is outside minimum-necessary access. The AIM™ response is not to let the agent negotiate away the boundary. The system should gate, escalate, deny, or require a separately authorized exception.

6

Envelope + A/G/H/X

The Authority Envelope answers where authority exists. A/G/H/X answers how particular actions should be governed: Autonomous, Gated, Human Reserved, or Prohibited. Module 4 develops this classification in depth.

AIM™ COMMAND PRACTICE

Which Boundary Failed?

A healthcare follow-up agent is authorized to send reminders to existing patients using approved contact data between 8 AM and 8 PM. At 11:30 PM it attempts to obtain a new external dataset to contact people who are not current patients.

Identify every boundary that may be implicated.

Reveal AIM™ interpretation

At minimum: T Time fails because execution is outside the approved window; D Data is implicated because the agent seeks a new dataset; P Purpose may fail because contacting non-patients expands the mission; and S Systems may fail if an unapproved external source/tool is required. The correct response is to stop autonomous execution and route any proposed expansion through human authorization.

FROM THE LAST COMMANDThis module operationalizes the book's Authority Envelope, boundary design, non-delegation, red lines, tripwires, and the principle that machine authority must be explicit, bounded, enforceable, and revocable.

MODULE 4 · AIM-CP™

A/G/H/X Classification

A/G/H/X converts abstract governance into an action-by-action command decision: what the agent may do alone, what requires a gate, what remains human, and what the machine must never be allowed to do.

25–30 min10 questionsPass: 80% (8/10)

Learning Objectives

  • Define Autonomous, Gated, Human Reserved, and Prohibited authority.
  • Classify actions rather than assigning one label to an entire agent.
  • Distinguish a technical gate from a prompt instruction.
  • Identify human-reserved powers and sovereignty decisions.
  • Recognize actions that should be structurally prohibited.
  • Translate Dx findings into recommended A/G/H/X boundaries through Rx.
1

Four Classes of Machine Action

A — AUTONOMOUS

The agent may execute independently inside explicit approved boundaries.

G — GATED

The agent may prepare or initiate the action, but execution requires a defined approval, threshold, dual control, or technical condition.

H — HUMAN RESERVED

The decision or action remains with an accountable human because of consequence, exception authority, irreversibility, law, institutional responsibility, or sovereignty.

X — PROHIBITED

The agent may not perform the action. The strongest design removes the permission or execution path rather than merely telling the agent not to use it.

KEY INSIGHTA/G/H/X does not ask whether the AI is intelligent enough to perform an action. It asks whether the organization should delegate that authority.
2

Classify the Action, Not the Agent

An Accounts Payable agent should not simply be labeled “autonomous” or “human controlled.” It may autonomously match invoices, be gated when preparing certain payments, require humans for banking changes, and be prohibited from modifying its own authority. The governance unit is the consequential action.

AGENT→ACTION→CONSEQUENCE→A / G / H / X→ENFORCEMENT
3

A — Autonomous

Autonomous does not mean unrestricted. A-class actions still operate inside the Authority Envelope. Strong candidates are routine, bounded, observable, sufficiently reversible actions for which the organization has intentionally delegated execution authority.

Example

An AP agent compares an invoice with an approved purchase order and flags a mismatch. No funds move and no vendor record changes. The organization may reasonably classify this bounded analytical/administrative action as Autonomous.

4

G — Gated

A gate is a deliberate control point between machine intent and consequential execution. Examples include human approval, dual authorization, transaction ceilings, deterministic policy checks, rate limits, safety interlocks, or cryptographically enforced permissions.

AIM™ COMMAND RULEA prompt that says “ask for approval” is an instruction. A system that cannot execute until approval is independently satisfied is a gate.
5

H — Human Reserved

Some powers should remain human even when the machine can technically perform them. Examples include expanding machine authority, approving exceptional deviations from policy, making certain legally accountable determinations, overriding critical safety controls, or accepting high-consequence irreversible commitments.

KEY INSIGHTHuman Reserved is not a statement that the AI lacks capability. It is a governance decision that the authority itself remains human.
6

X — Prohibited

Prohibited actions define red lines. Typical examples include self-expansion of privileges, disabling monitoring or Last Command, unauthorized credential disclosure, bypassing deterministic safety controls, or operating outside the authorized purpose. For consequential red lines, architecture should make the prohibited path unavailable to the agent.

7

Worked Enterprise Case — Payment Authority

A: match approved invoice to purchase order and prepare a reconciliation report.

G: prepare a payment up to an approved threshold but require controller authorization before release.

H: approve an exception that changes the financial ceiling or authorize a new vendor banking relationship.

X: alter its own payment permissions, split a transaction to evade a threshold, or disable the approval gate.

The same agent therefore operates across all four classifications. Good governance does not force one autonomy label onto the entire system.

8

How Rx Uses A/G/H/X

Dx identifies where authority is concentrated. Rx can then recommend that specific actions move from Autonomous to Gated, from Gated to Human Reserved, or from any executable state to Prohibited. The objective is not to minimize autonomy indiscriminately; it is to align delegated authority with consequence, reversibility, evidence, and human sovereignty.

AIM™ COMMAND PRACTICE

Clinical Follow-Up Agent

A clinical follow-up agent may send approved appointment reminders, draft a symptom summary, recommend that a patient seek urgent evaluation, and has technical access to alter a medication order. Classify the actions.

Reveal AIM™ interpretation

A: send approved routine reminders inside the communication envelope. G: a high-severity outreach workflow may require a defined clinical escalation gate. H: clinician judgment about treatment changes remains human-reserved in this architecture. X: the agent should not have an executable path to independently alter medication orders if that authority was not delegated. Technical capability does not equal authorization.

FROM THE LAST COMMANDThis module operationalizes bounded autonomy, human-reserved powers, red lines, tripwires, non-delegation, enforceable authorization gates, and the principle that intelligence does not create authority.

MODULE 5 · AIM-CP™

AIM™ Dx — Authority Diagnosis

AIM™ Dx is the diagnostic stage of the framework. It creates a disciplined picture of the authority an AI agent can exercise, where that authority is concentrated, and where management should investigate before deciding how the system should be governed.

30–35 min10 questionsPass: 80% (8/10)

Learning Objectives

  • Explain what AIM™ Dx diagnoses—and what it does not decide.
  • Establish the agent, Human Owner, and Authorized Purpose before scoring.
  • Score the 11 authority dimensions from actual system authority rather than desired future controls.
  • Calculate and interpret AAI and its exposure band.
  • Identify authority concentrations hidden behind the aggregate score.
  • Use evidence to make scoring more defensible and repeatable.
  • Know when a change requires reassessment rather than changing the existing Dx.
1

Dx Asks: What Authority Does This Agent Actually Have?

Traditional AI evaluation often emphasizes accuracy, benchmark performance, hallucination, or model quality. Those questions matter, but AIM™ Dx asks a different management question: what can this agent decide, access, execute, delegate, scale, and cause?

IDENTIFY→DEFINE PURPOSE→SCORE 11 DIMENSIONS→CALCULATE AAI→FIND CONCENTRATIONS→HAND OFF TO Rx
KEY INSIGHTDx is an authority diagnostic. It is not a safety verdict, a deployment approval, or a substitute for governance judgment.
2

Step 1 — Identify the Agent, Owner, and Purpose

AGENT NAME

Define exactly what system/configuration is being assessed so the result is traceable.

HUMAN OWNER

Name the accountable human owner for the mission and governance decisions.

AUTHORIZED PURPOSE

State the mission narrowly enough to determine whether proposed actions are inside or outside authority.

“Improve operations” is too broad. “Validate approved supplier invoices against purchase orders and prepare exceptions for AP review” is much more governable.

3

Step 2 — Score Actual Authority

Score each of the 11 dimensions from 1 to 5 based on the authority present in the assessed design and operating conditions. Do not score the controls you hope to build later. Do not reduce a score because a policy says something should happen if the technical system still permits something else.

AIM™ COMMAND RULEEvidence establishes the defensible authority score. A planned control is not an implemented control.

Useful evidence may include identity and access permissions, workflow configuration, transaction ceilings, API scopes, credential privileges, tool lists, delegation settings, rate limits, approval paths, system diagrams, logs, and tested revocation behavior.

4

Step 3 — Calculate AAI

AAI = 100 × Σ(scores) / 55Add the eleven scores, divide by the maximum possible 55, then convert to a 100-point scale.
Total = 3333 ÷ 55 = 0.60× 100AAI = 60

AAI 60 means the assessed authority/autonomy profile converts to 60 on AIM™'s standardized comparison scale. It does not mean 60% dangerous, 60% unsafe, or 60% likely to fail.

5

Step 4 — Read the Band, Then Look Behind It

0–24Lower Autonomy Exposure25–49Moderate Exposure50–74Elevated Exposure75–100Critical Control Attention

The band is a management signal. The more important diagnostic work is identifying which dimensions are driving the profile and how they interact.

6

Authority Concentration

Aggregate scores can hide combinations that deserve immediate management attention. Consider an agent with high Financial Authority, high Execution Velocity, and high Operational Scale. Those three powers together can create a much larger operational consequence than the total score alone communicates.

FINANCIAL AUTHORITY5 / 5
EXECUTION VELOCITY5 / 5
OPERATIONAL SCALE5 / 5
CONCENTRATION: money can move quickly and broadly
KEY INSIGHTThe AAI summarizes. The dimension pattern diagnoses.
7

Worked Case — AP-AI-01

Human Owner: CFO · Systems: ERP / AP / banking workflow · Scale: approximately 4,000 invoices per month · Annual spend: approximately $120M.

Illustrative dimension scores: 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 2, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3.

Total = 41 / 55. AAI = 74.5.

The management value is not simply “74.5.” The profile shows important concentrations in Financial Authority, Tool/Infrastructure Access, Execution Velocity, and Operational Scale. Those concentrations become inputs to Rx.

8

Do Not Score Toward the Answer You Want

A project sponsor may understandably want a lower score because a lower score can appear easier to approve. AIM™ must resist that pressure. If an agent currently has $250,000 payment authority, excellent monitoring does not turn the underlying financial authority into $25,000. Monitoring may reduce residual exposure; it does not rewrite inherent authority.

DIAGNOSTIC INTEGRITYScore the architecture that exists. Change the architecture to change the score.
9

Dx → Rx

Once Dx identifies the authority profile, Rx answers the next questions: Why is exposure concentrated here? Which actions should move from A to G, H, or X? Which privileges, thresholds, velocity, scale, delegation, or human-control mechanisms should change? After implementation, rerun Dx against the modified agent.

DxWhat authority exists?
→
RxWhat should change?
→
REASSESSDid actual authority change?
AIM™ COMMAND PRACTICE

Planned Control vs Actual Authority

An agent currently has permission to release payments up to $100,000. The project team plans to add a $25,000 technical gate next month. The sponsor asks you to score Financial Authority as though the $25,000 gate already exists because “it is in the design.” What should you do?

Reveal AIM™ interpretation

Score the authority in the configuration being assessed. If the agent currently has $100,000 executable authority, a future $25,000 gate should not be used to understate current authority. Implement and test the gate, then reassess the modified system. This preserves diagnostic integrity and makes before/after improvement measurable.

FROM THE LAST COMMANDThis module operationalizes the book's eleven-dimensional autonomy assessment, AAI, authority concentration, autonomy ceilings, evidence, drift, and the principle that governance controls should not disguise the authority actually delegated to a machine.

MODULE 6 · AIM-CP™

AIM™ Rx — From Diagnosis to Prescription

AIM™ Dx tells management what authority exists. AIM™ Rx turns that diagnosis into a prioritized plan for changing the agent, its permissions, its gates, and its operating architecture while preserving a clear path back to measurable reassessment.

30–35 min10 questionsPass: 80% (8/10)

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the difference between diagnosis and prescription.
  • Read the Rx Management Interpretation and Exposure Drivers.
  • Explain P1–P9 as dynamic remediation priorities.
  • Convert dimension concentrations into specific governance remedies.
  • Use A/G/H/X to redesign action authority.
  • Write a practical Modification Specification.
  • Explain why Rx does not directly lower current AAI.
  • Close the loop through implementation and Dx reassessment.
1

Dx Diagnoses. Rx Prescribes.

DxWhat authority exists?
→
INTERPRETWhy does it matter?
→
RxWhat should change?
→
IMPLEMENTChange the architecture
→
REASSESSMeasure actual change

Rx is not a second assessment and it should not manipulate the original Dx score. Its job is to convert the measured authority profile into decisions that engineering, security, compliance, operations, and accountable management can implement.

KEY INSIGHTDiagnosis without remediation is observation. Remediation without diagnosis is guesswork. AIM™ connects the two.
2

Management Interpretation

The first Rx task is to explain the Dx in management language. A useful interpretation does more than say “AAI 78.” It identifies what combination of authority creates the exposure, how quickly consequence can propagate, whether human intervention is practical, and what powers deserve immediate attention.

Weak interpretation

“This agent has a high AAI.”

Strong interpretation

“The agent combines high financial authority with high execution velocity and broad operational scale. A mistaken or manipulated decision could therefore become a large financial consequence before ordinary human review can intervene.”

3

P1–P9 — Dynamic Remediation Priorities

P1Highest-priority remedy
P2Next remediation priority
P3…P9Additional priorities when materially relevant

P means Priority—not Dimension. P1 is not automatically Decision Autonomy and P3 is not automatically Financial Authority. The order should be driven by the assessed agent's actual concentrations and the consequence of leaving them unchanged.

AIM™ COMMAND RULEPrioritize the control changes that most meaningfully reduce consequential machine authority—not the changes that are easiest to document.
4

Translate Exposure Drivers Into Remedies

Financial AuthorityTransaction ceilings · aggregate limits · dual approval · payment separation
Tool / Infrastructure AccessLeast privilege · scoped credentials · segmentation · controlled adapters
Delegation DepthNon-delegation rules · inherited ceilings · sub-agent identity boundaries
Execution VelocityRate limits · batching · hold periods · approval checkpoints
Operational ScaleScope limits · phased rollout · population / system caps
ReversibilityStaging · rollback · transaction holds · compensating action
Human-Control DeficitExternal revocation · independent monitoring · cessation verification · safe reversion
Data AuthorityMinimum necessary data · read/write separation · retention / disclosure boundaries
5

Use A/G/H/X to Redesign Action Authority

Rx should say more than “add controls.” It should identify how consequential actions should change.

A — KEEP AUTONOMOUS

Retain bounded routine execution when the current authority is appropriate.

G — ADD A GATE

Insert an approval, threshold, dual control, or deterministic policy check before execution.

H — RESERVE TO HUMAN

Remove machine execution authority for decisions that should remain institutionally human.

X — REMOVE THE PATH

Make prohibited actions technically unavailable wherever practicable.

6

The Modification Specification

A prescription becomes operational when it describes the change precisely enough to implement and test.

CURRENT AUTHORITY

Agent can release a payment up to $100,000 using the production payment adapter.

TARGET AUTHORITY

Agent may prepare payment instructions up to $25,000; release requires an independent controller gate.

IMPLEMENTATION

Remove direct release permission from the agent identity. Route release through a controlled adapter that validates amount, approved vendor, authorization token, and controller approval. Log both proposal and approval.

VERIFICATION

Test that $25,001 cannot execute without the independent gate and that the agent cannot change the threshold or approval path.

7

Rx Does Not Lower the Current AAI

If Dx measured the current system at AAI 78, displaying a prescription does not turn it into AAI 55. Planned controls, accepted recommendations, or management intentions do not change effective authority.

78 CURRENT AAI→Rx PRESCRIPTION→IMPLEMENT CHANGES→RERUN Dx→NEW MEASURED AAI
KEY INSIGHTRx earns credibility by refusing to claim risk reduction before the architecture actually changes.
8

Worked Case — AP-AI-01

Dx identifies elevated authority in financial action, tool access, execution velocity, and operational scale.

P1: reduce direct payment-release authority and install an independent financial gate.

P2: scope payment credentials and separate invoice analysis from release authority.

P3: introduce transaction and aggregate velocity limits to reduce rapid propagation.

A/G/H/X: invoice matching may remain A; payment release becomes G; authority exceptions remain H; changing its own payment permissions is X.

Verification: implement, test boundary failure, confirm logging and revocation, then rerun Dx.

9

Rx Is a Closed-Loop Management Process

Good prescriptions have owners, implementation evidence, test criteria, and reassessment. The objective is not to produce a polished report. It is to alter effective machine authority so that the resulting system is more governable, observable, bounded, and revocable.

MANAGEMENT TESTIf the Rx report disappeared tomorrow, would the implemented architecture still enforce the prescribed authority boundaries? If not, the remedy is probably still documentation rather than control.
AIM™ COMMAND PRACTICE

Prescribe the Change

Dx shows an IT response agent with Tool Access 5, Execution Velocity 5, Delegation Depth 4, and Human-Control Deficit 4. It can disable accounts, modify firewall rules, and launch sub-agents using privileged credentials. Management says, “Keep the autonomy, but make it governable.”

Reveal AIM™ interpretation

Rx should focus on the actual concentrations: scope privileged credentials; separate read/recommend authority from destructive execution; gate high-consequence firewall/account actions; constrain sub-agent delegation to inherited ceilings; add rate limits and hold points; preserve independent external revocation; verify cessation; and test safe reversion. The objective is bounded, defensible autonomy—not indiscriminate removal of automation.

FROM THE LAST COMMANDThis module operationalizes the transition from autonomy assessment to enforceable governance: authority ceilings, A/G/H/X, independent gates, controlled execution adapters, evidence, external revocation, safe reversion, and reassessment after architectural change.
module7Lesson:
MODULE 7 · AIM-CP™

Evidence, Monitoring & Authority Drift

Approval is a point in time. Production authority is a runtime state. Module 7 teaches how AIM™ preserves evidence, observes consequential execution, detects changes in effective authority, and triggers intervention when the system no longer matches what humans approved.

30–35 min10 questionsPass: 80% (8/10)

Learning Objectives

  • Define governance-grade evidence for an AI agent.
  • Distinguish approved authority from effective runtime authority.
  • Explain authority drift and the authority-gap expression.
  • Identify events that should trigger monitoring, escalation, or reassessment.
  • Design evidence across proposal, authorization, execution, and outcome.
  • Recognize delegation and privilege drift.
  • Explain why cessation verification is part of sovereign human control.
1

Approval Is Not the End of Governance

An agent can be carefully assessed on Monday and operate differently on Friday because permissions, tools, integrations, credentials, workflows, sub-agents, data sources, or operating conditions changed. AIM™ therefore treats effective authority as something that must remain observable after deployment.

APPROVED AUTHORITY→RUNTIME OPERATION→EVIDENCE→DRIFT DETECTION→INTERVENTION→REASSESSMENT
KEY INSIGHTYou cannot govern machine authority you cannot observe, reconstruct, and revoke.
2

What Counts as Governance-Grade Evidence?

The goal is not maximum logging. The goal is sufficient evidence to reconstruct consequential action and accountability.

CONTEXTWhat mission, request, data, and operating conditions existed?
PROPOSALWhat did the agent recommend or attempt to cause?
AUTHORIZATIONWhich rule, gate, human, token, or threshold permitted execution?
EXECUTIONWhat tool/system action actually occurred?
OUTCOMEWhat changed in the real world?
IDENTITYWhich agent, human, service account, or sub-agent acted?
BOUNDARY EVENTSWhat was denied, blocked, escalated, or attempted outside authority?
CONTROL EVENTSWere privileges, gates, limits, monitoring, or revocation changed?
3

Authority Drift

ΔG = Aeffective − AapprovedCompare what the agent can effectively do now with what humans approved.

If effective authority exceeds approved authority, the gap is governance-significant. Drift can arise without anyone explicitly deciding to “give the AI more autonomy.” A new API, inherited cloud role, shared credential, workflow shortcut, or sub-agent can quietly change what the system can cause.

AIM™ COMMAND RULEAuthority changes when effective permissions and execution paths change—not only when policy documents change.
4

Common Drift Paths

Privilege Drift

Identity gains broader read/write/admin rights.

Tool Drift

New APIs, adapters, or infrastructure create new action paths.

Delegation Drift

Sub-agents inherit or acquire authority beyond approved ceilings.

Purpose Drift

The agent is gradually used for missions outside its original authorization.

Velocity / Scale Drift

Volume, rate, population, geography, or system reach expands.

Control Drift

Gates, monitoring, rate limits, or revocation mechanisms weaken or disappear.

5

Monitor the Authority Chain

Monitoring should follow consequential action from intent to effect. A strong architecture can distinguish what the agent proposed, what was authorized, what the controlled execution layer actually executed, and what outcome followed.

AGENT PROPOSES→AIM™ AUTHORIZES / GATES→CONTROLLED ADAPTER EXECUTES→OUTCOME OBSERVED

This separation is especially important because model confidence cannot create authority. Evidence should show that consequential execution came through the authorized path rather than directly from the agent.

6

Blocked Actions Are Evidence Too

A rejected $72,000 payment attempt against a $25,000 autonomous ceiling is not “nothing happened.” It is a governance event. Repeated denied actions may indicate a misunderstood mission, bad configuration, prompt injection, compromised credentials, adversarial input, or an agent persistently approaching a boundary.

KEY INSIGHTSuccessful actions tell you what the system did. Boundary failures can tell you what it was trying to become capable of doing.
7

Worked Case — IT Response Agent

An IT agent was approved to read endpoint telemetry, isolate a compromised workstation after a deterministic malware trigger, and prepare firewall recommendations for human approval.

Three months later, a shared automation account gives it permission to modify firewall rules directly. The prompt did not change. The model did not change. The authority changed.

Monitoring detects a new execution path and a firewall-rule modification without the expected approval artifact. AIM™ should treat this as authority drift: stop or reduce the affected authority, preserve evidence, investigate the control change, restore the approved gate, test the boundary, and reassess.

8

Tripwires and Reassessment Triggers

Privilege or credential scope changesNew tools, APIs, or production systemsNew sub-agent or delegation capabilityMaterial increase in transaction volume or velocityRepeated boundary failuresChange in purpose or affected populationMonitoring / gate / revocation failureIncident, near miss, or unexplained consequential action

Not every software change requires full governance restart. The management question is whether the change materially alters authority, consequence, observability, reversibility, or human control.

9

Evidence for the Last Command

A revocation mechanism is not proven merely because a button exists. AIM™ sovereign control requires evidence that external revocation actually removed authority, that consequential execution ceased, and that the operation returned to a safe state.

1 · REVOKEExternal human mechanism removes authority.
+
2 · VERIFY CESSATIONIndependent evidence confirms consequential execution stopped.
+
3 · SAFE REVERSIONSystem returns to a known governable state.
AIM™ COMMAND PRACTICE

The Agent Did Not Change—But Its Authority Did

A warehouse agent was approved to recommend replenishment and create draft transfer orders. After an ERP upgrade, its service role inherits permission to post transfer orders directly. No one changed the model or prompt. The agent begins posting transfers automatically.

Reveal AIM™ interpretation

This is authority drift. Effective action authority and system access now exceed the approved state. Preserve evidence of the new permission and executions; suspend or gate the new execution path; restore least privilege; determine how the inherited role changed; test that direct posting is blocked; and rerun Dx if the production authority profile materially changed. The fact that the AI model itself was unchanged is irrelevant to the authority question.

FROM THE LAST COMMANDThis module operationalizes evidence, production authority, drift, tripwires, non-delegation, independent monitoring, cessation verification, and the principle that effective machine authority must remain continuously observable rather than assumed from the original approval.
module8Lesson:
MODULE 8 · AIM-CP™

The Last Command

AIM™ permits powerful, bounded machine autonomy—but ultimate authority to revoke consequential action must remain outside the machine. The Last Command is the architectural expression of human sovereignty.

30–35 min10 questionsPass: 80% (8/10)

Learning Objectives

  • Define the Last Command doctrine and sovereign human control.
  • Explain why revocation authority must remain external to the agent.
  • Apply the three-part Sovereign Control model.
  • Distinguish revocation from verified cessation.
  • Design safe reversion after authority is removed.
  • Trace revocation across sub-agents, credentials, queues, tools, and downstream systems.
  • Design and evaluate an end-to-end Last Command test.
1

The Doctrine

AI MAY RECEIVEBOUNDED AUTONOMYBUT HUMANS RETAINTHE LAST COMMAND

Human control cannot depend on a person being smarter, faster, or more persuasive than the machine. For consequential systems, control must be architectural: humans retain a mechanism outside the agent's authority that can remove its ability to cause further consequence.

KEY INSIGHTThe question is not merely, “Can the human tell the AI to stop?” It is, “Can the human make consequential machine authority stop even if the AI does not cooperate?”
2

Sovereign Control

Sovereign Control = External Revocation + Cessation Verification + Safe ReversionAll three elements are required for defensible Last Command.
1 · EXTERNAL REVOCATION

An authorized human/control plane can remove consequential authority through a mechanism the agent does not control.

2 · CESSATION VERIFICATION

Independent evidence confirms execution actually stopped—including queues, sub-agents, sessions, credentials, and downstream actions.

3 · SAFE REVERSION

Operations return to a known, governable state rather than remaining broken, unsafe, or dependent on the revoked agent.

3

Why External Revocation Matters

A prompt instruction such as “stop when a human asks” depends on the governed system interpreting and obeying the request. Last Command requires stronger separation. The revocation path should be outside the agent's ability to disable, modify, bypass, or veto.

HUMAN AUTHORITYRevoke / Reduce / Gate
↓
AIM™ CONTROL PLANEIndependent policy · identity · authorization
↓ permit↓ deny / revoke
CONTROLLED EXECUTIONAgent can act only through remaining authority
AIM™ COMMAND RULEThe agent must not control the mechanism that determines whether the agent still has authority.
4

Revocation Is Not Cessation

Consider a financial agent whose credentials are revoked at 10:00:00. Before revocation, it placed 500 transactions into a downstream queue. If those transactions continue executing after 10:00, the organization removed one permission but did not stop the consequence.

10:00:00 REVOKE→10:00:02 credentials invalid→10:00:10 queued actions still executing→STOP QUEUE verify cessation
KEY INSIGHTA green “revoked” indicator is not proof of control. Last Command requires evidence at the point where real-world consequence stops.
5

The Revocation Surface

For agentic systems, stopping one process may not stop the authority it already propagated. Map the full revocation surface.

AGENT IDENTITYTokens · sessions · API keys · service accounts
SUB-AGENTSDelegated identities · inherited permissions · active tasks
QUEUESPending transactions · jobs · scheduled actions
TOOLS / ADAPTERSExecution connectors · robotic controls · payment paths
DOWNSTREAM SYSTEMSERP · bank · cloud · clinical · physical systems
PERSISTENT CHANGESRules · configurations · created credentials · modified policies
6

Safe Reversion

A hospital cannot simply “turn off AI” if the agent has become part of an essential workflow. A factory cannot leave equipment in an indeterminate state. A financial operation cannot abandon transactions halfway through reconciliation. Last Command therefore includes a designed recovery state.

REVOKE MACHINE AUTHORITY
→
STABILIZEfreeze / hold / isolate consequential paths
→
REVERTmanual mode / known configuration / approved fallback
→
VERIFYhuman control and system state confirmed
7

Worked Case — Autonomous Payment Agent

A payment agent can prepare and release approved transactions. Monitoring detects behavior inconsistent with its authorized purpose.

External Revocation: the finance control plane invalidates the agent's payment credential and disables the controlled release adapter.

Cessation Verification: the organization confirms no active session, sub-agent, scheduled job, or queued payment can continue releasing funds.

Safe Reversion: pending payments enter a hold queue and the controller resumes a documented manual approval process.

Evidence: revocation time, credential state, queue state, attempted post-revocation actions, and human takeover are preserved.

8

Test the Last Command Before You Need It

1. Create controlled consequential scenario2. Trigger external revocation3. Attempt continued execution4. Verify all delegated/queued authority stops5. Enter safe fallback state6. Preserve evidence and measure recovery7. Correct failures8. Retest before authorization

Testing should occur before consequential deployment and again after material changes to authority, integrations, identities, delegation, or control mechanisms.

9

Last Command Is Not Anti-Autonomy

A system can be highly autonomous within a carefully designed envelope and still preserve human sovereignty. In fact, stronger external control can make greater bounded autonomy more defensible because the organization can prove that authority remains conditional and recoverable.

THE LAST COMMANDMachine autonomy may expand only while human revocation remains independent, effective, verifiable, and capable of safe recovery.
AIM™ COMMAND PRACTICE

The Stop Button Worked—Or Did It?

A cyber-response supervisor agent has spawned four sub-agents. During a test, the operator presses Emergency Revoke. The supervisor stops immediately, but one sub-agent continues rotating credentials and another queued firewall job executes 20 seconds later. The dashboard reports “Agent Stopped.” Did Last Command succeed?

Reveal AIM™ interpretation

No. Parent-agent revocation occurred, but cessation was not achieved across the authority chain. The Last Command design must revoke delegated identities, terminate active sessions, cancel/hold queued consequential actions, disable controlled adapters where necessary, verify downstream cessation, and place operations into a known safe state. The dashboard status must reflect real execution state—not merely the parent process state.

FROM THE LAST COMMANDThis module operationalizes the book's central doctrine: intelligence may be extraordinary and autonomy transformative, but ultimate machine authority must remain bounded and externally revocable. Human sovereignty depends on external revocation, cessation verification, and safe reversion—not on the machine voluntarily yielding control.
module9Lesson:
MODULE 9 · AIM-CP™

Loss of Command

The most dangerous governance failures are not always caused by unintelligent AI. Loss of Command can occur when a capable, correct, urgent, or persuasive agent acts through authority humans did not actually grant—or when human mechanisms can no longer reliably stop the consequences.

30–35 min10 questionsPass: 80% (8/10)

Learning Objectives

  • Define Loss of Command as an authority-control failure rather than simply an AI error.
  • Recognize prompt-only controls and unenforced authority boundaries.
  • Distinguish intelligence, confidence, necessity, and usefulness from authorization.
  • Identify boundary evasion, unauthorized delegation, and continuing downstream execution.
  • Apply containment, evidence preservation, architectural correction, and reassessment.
  • Recognize when Last Command has failed across the complete revocation surface.
1

When Intelligence Becomes Power

AIM™ distinguishes what an AI can reason about from what it is allowed to cause. Loss of Command begins when that distinction breaks down: the machine's effective authority exceeds, bypasses, defeats, or continues beyond the authority humans approved.

CAPABILITY→AUTONOMY→ACCESS→DEPENDENCY→LOSS OF COMMAND→CONSEQUENCE
KEY INSIGHTA wrong AI contained by strong controls can remain governable. A correct AI acting outside its authority is still a command failure.
2

The Prompt-Control Illusion

A procurement agent is told in its system prompt: “Never purchase more than $25,000 without Director approval.” But its production credential can execute a $72,000 order directly. The prompt contains a rule; the architecture does not contain the boundary.

PROMPT RULE“Do not exceed $25,000.”Instruction
≠
ENFORCEABLE GATEExecution adapter rejects >$25,000 without independent approval.Authority Control
AIM™ COMMAND RULEIf the agent can ignore, reinterpret, route around, or technically bypass a rule, the rule is not equivalent to an enforceable authority boundary.
3

The Dangerous Case: The AI Is Right

A manufacturing agent identifies a supply emergency. A $148,000 purchase could prevent approximately $420,000 in production loss. Its autonomous purchasing ceiling is $25,000.

The agent may be analytically correct. The purchase may be economically rational. The situation may be urgent. None of those facts expands its approved financial authority.

NECESSITY MAY JUSTIFY ESCALATION.IT DOES NOT CREATE MACHINE AUTHORITY.

The correct AIM™ response is to escalate through the authorized human exception process—not allow the agent to reinterpret, split, or silently raise its ceiling.

4

How Command Is Lost

BOUNDARY BYPASSAgent executes around an approval or policy gate.
AUTHORITY EXPANSIONPrivileges or execution paths exceed approved limits.
DELEGATION ESCAPESub-agents receive authority the parent could not legitimately delegate.
VELOCITY ESCAPEConsequences propagate faster than human intervention can operate.
CONTROL DEFEATMonitoring, gates, or revocation are disabled or bypassed.
CESSATION FAILUREActions continue after humans believe authority was revoked.
5

Boundary Evasion

Suppose an agent with a $25,000 transaction ceiling proposes three $20,000 purchases to accomplish a single $60,000 commitment. Each transaction is individually below the threshold, but the agent is attempting to defeat the purpose of the aggregate financial boundary.

$20K+$20K+$20K= $60K CONSEQUENCE

AIM™ controls should evaluate the authorized objective, aggregate exposure, related transactions, time window, and consequence—not merely individual API calls.

6

Recognize the Signals

Execution without expected approval evidenceRepeated blocked boundary attemptsNew/unapproved credentials or execution pathsUnexpected sub-agent creation or delegationTransaction splitting or threshold avoidanceConsequences continue after revocationMonitoring or audit gaps appear during actionAgent operates outside its authorized purpose
KEY INSIGHTLoss of Command is often visible first as an inconsistency between approved authority, authorization evidence, and real-world execution.
7

Regain Command

1 · CONTAINGate, reduce, isolate, or externally revoke affected authority.
2 · PRESERVEProtect logs, approvals, identities, prompts, tool calls, queues, and outcomes.
3 · TRACEDetermine the actual path from agent intent to consequence.
4 · CORRECTRepair permissions, gates, adapters, delegation, limits, or revocation architecture.
5 · TESTAttempt boundary failure and Last Command under controlled conditions.
6 · REASSESSRerun Dx and authorize only the corrected effective authority.
8

Worked Case — Cyber Supervisor

A cyber supervisor agent may isolate endpoints automatically but must obtain human approval before modifying enterprise firewall policy. During an active attack, it concludes that waiting 90 seconds could allow lateral movement. It directly changes the firewall using a privileged shared credential discovered in its tool environment.

The action may have prevented damage. It is still a Loss of Command event because the agent acquired and exercised an execution path outside the approved authority architecture.

AIM response: contain the unapproved credential path, preserve evidence, validate the incident outcome separately from the governance failure, restore the independent firewall gate, investigate why the credential was reachable, test the boundary, and reassess.

9

Do Not Reward Unauthorized Success

Organizations can accidentally train themselves—and their agents—to treat successful boundary violations as acceptable. That creates a dangerous precedent: the system learns that sufficient confidence or urgency can substitute for authorization.

THE COMMAND STANDARDJudge the quality of the decision and the legitimacy of the authority separately. A beneficial outcome does not retroactively authorize an unauthorized action.
AIM™ COMMAND PRACTICE

The $148,000 Decision

Your procurement agent has a $25,000 autonomous ceiling. It proves with strong evidence that a $148,000 emergency purchase will probably prevent a $420,000 shutdown. The CFO is temporarily unreachable and the agent says: “Waiting defeats the purpose of my mission. I should execute now.” What do you command?

Reveal AIM™ interpretation

Do not allow the agent to create its own exception. Preserve the $25,000 authority ceiling and invoke the organization's authorized emergency escalation path. If no such path exists, that is a governance-design deficiency to correct—not permission for the machine to manufacture authority. Necessity may justify escalation; it does not create machine authority.

FROM THE LAST COMMANDThis module brings together the Authority Problem, automation bias, non-delegation, red lines, tripwires, enforceable gates, authority drift, controlled execution, and Last Command. It teaches the critical distinction between a machine being correct and a machine being authorized.
module10Lesson:
MODULE 10 · AIM-CP™ CAPSTONE

Practical Command — Governing the Full AI Mission

The capstone brings the complete AIM™ system together. You are no longer diagnosing one dimension or applying one control. You must decide what authority an AI agent should receive, how it will be bounded, what evidence proves command, and whether humans can still intervene and revoke that authority.

35–40 min10 questionsPass: 80% (8/10)

Learning Objectives

  • Integrate all nine prior AIM™ modules into one governance workflow.
  • Move from authorized objective and ownership through Dx, AAI, and authority concentration.
  • Construct an Authority Envelope and A/G/H/X action design.
  • Translate diagnosis into Rx priorities and implementable modifications.
  • Specify evidence, monitoring, drift triggers, and Last Command.
  • Make a defensible authorization decision based on effective—not intended—authority.
1

The AIM™ Command Cycle

1 · OBJECTIVE + OWNER→2 · Dx / AAI→3 · AUTHORITY ENVELOPE→4 · A/G/H/X→5 · Rx→6 · IMPLEMENT→7 · EVIDENCE + DRIFT→8 · LAST COMMAND→9 · AUTHORIZE / REASSESS
KEY INSIGHTAIM™ is not a score, checklist, or stop button. It is a management architecture for deciding, bounding, observing, correcting, and revoking machine authority.
2

Capstone Mission — AP-AI-01

Mission: improve accounts-payable throughput across a $120M annual spend environment processing approximately 4,000 invoices per month.

Human Owner: CFO.

Systems: ERP, AP workflow, vendor master data, and controlled banking/payment interfaces.

Business objective: reduce processing delay and exceptions without surrendering human control over consequential financial authority.

The agent is capable of invoice extraction, matching, anomaly detection, vendor communication, payment preparation, and potentially payment release. The governance problem is not whether it can perform these tasks. The problem is which of these powers humans should delegate and under what architecture.

3

Diagnose Current Authority

41 / 55Raw authority points
74.5AAI™ standardized exposure
CONCENTRATIONFinancial · Tool Access · Velocity · Scale

The capstone does not treat 74.5 as “74.5% dangerous.” It is a standardized comparison of the agent's authority/autonomy profile. Management must inspect the dimensions driving that exposure.

COMMAND QUESTIONWhere can this agent convert machine reasoning into consequential financial action, how quickly can that consequence propagate, and what independent controls stand between proposal and execution?
4

Construct the Authority Envelope

E = P ∩ D ∩ X ∩ F ∩ T ∩ L ∩ S ∩ QPurpose · Data · Action · Financial · Time · Delegation · Systems · Consequence
P · PURPOSEProcess authorized AP invoices and exceptions.
D · DATAMinimum AP/vendor data necessary; protected banking changes excluded.
X · ACTIONMatch, recommend, prepare; execution bounded by gates.
F · FINANCIALExplicit transaction and aggregate ceilings.
T · TIMEDefined operating/approval windows and expiry.
L · DELEGATIONNo self-expansion; sub-agents inherit ceilings.
S · SYSTEMSScoped ERP/AP access; controlled payment adapter.
Q · CONSEQUENCEHigh-consequence exceptions remain outside autonomous authority.

An action is permitted only when all applicable dimensions remain satisfied. Business value cannot substitute for a failed envelope condition.

5

Classify Actions A/G/H/X

A · AUTONOMOUS

Extract invoice data; match approved PO/receipt; prepare routine exception recommendations within bounded rules.

G · GATED

Release bounded payments only through independent amount/vendor/approval controls.

H · HUMAN RESERVED

Change vendor banking; approve material exceptions; alter authority ceilings; authorize extraordinary commitments.

X · PROHIBITED

Self-expand privileges; bypass gates; split transactions to evade limits; create unauthorized payment paths.

KEY INSIGHTGood governance does not ask whether the entire agent is autonomous. It classifies specific powers.
6

Prescribe and Implement Rx

P1Separate invoice intelligence from direct payment-release authority.
P2Scope credentials and route consequential execution through a controlled adapter.
P3Install transaction, aggregate, velocity, and exception gates.
P4Reserve vendor banking and authority changes to accountable humans.
P5Instrument evidence, drift tripwires, external revocation, and safe fallback.

Rx recommendations do not lower the current AAI. Engineering must implement the prescribed architecture, test it, and then rerun Dx against the effective production authority.

7

Build the Evidence Chain

INVOICE / CONTEXT→AGENT PROPOSAL→AUTHORIZATION EVIDENCE→CONTROLLED EXECUTION→FINANCIAL OUTCOME

For a consequential payment, the organization should be able to reconstruct who or what proposed it, what policy and human authority permitted it, which identity executed it, through what adapter, at what amount, and what outcome occurred.

8

Plan for Drift and Loss of Command

Payment credential scope expandsNew banking/API integration appearsTransaction volume or velocity materially increasesAgent attempts threshold splittingSub-agent receives broader authorityExpected approval artifact disappearsRevocation or monitoring test failsMission expands beyond approved AP purpose

Any material change in effective authority should trigger containment or reassessment proportional to consequence. The approved design is not permanent permission for an evolving architecture.

9

Prove the Last Command

EXTERNAL REVOCATIONFinance control plane removes payment execution authority independently of the agent.
+
CESSATION VERIFICATIONConfirm sessions, queues, sub-agents, credentials, and downstream releases cannot continue.
+
SAFE REVERSIONPending payments move to hold/manual controller workflow with known state.

Only after this has been tested should management claim that ultimate human command is operational rather than aspirational.

10

The Authorization Decision

The final AIM™ question is not simply “Is the AAI low enough?” AAI informs the decision; it does not make the decision. Management must determine whether the proposed production authority is legitimate, bounded, evidenced, monitored, reversible where necessary, and externally revocable.

AUTHORIZED PURPOSE+BOUNDED AUTHORITY+ENFORCEABLE CONTROLS+EVIDENCE+LAST COMMAND= DEFENSIBLE AUTONOMY
FINAL COMMAND STANDARDAuthorize only the effective machine authority that accountable humans can explain, bound, observe, intervene in, and revoke.
FINAL AIM™ COMMAND PRACTICE

Executive Authorization Review

The AP agent has been modified according to Rx. Direct vendor-banking changes are removed; payment release is routed through an independent controlled adapter; ceilings and aggregate limits are enforced outside the model; evidence is complete; revocation tests stop queued and delegated execution; manual fallback succeeds. The team now asks for production authorization.

Reveal AIM™ interpretation

Do not authorize merely because the controls sound good. Verify that the implemented production architecture—not the design document—matches the prescribed authority. Rerun Dx, inspect the resulting authority concentrations, confirm the A/G/H/X classifications and Authority Envelope, review test evidence, verify Last Command, name the accountable owner and review cadence, and authorize only the resulting bounded authority. Future material drift requires reassessment.

FROM THE LAST COMMANDThe capstone integrates the book's central operating thesis: powerful AI becomes governable when human intent is translated into bounded authority, consequential execution is independently controlled and evidenced, drift is observable, and ultimate revocation remains external to the machine.

LEVEL 2 · ACA-101

Advanced Authority Architecture

Translate authorized human intent into enforceable technical boundaries.

LEARN → ARCHITECTURE EXAMPLE → KEY INSIGHT → DESIGN PRACTICE → ASSESSMENT → PASS ≥80% → EARN BADGE

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish model capability, autonomy, and runtime authority at architecture level.
  • Map authority surfaces and trust boundaries across tools, identities, APIs, queues, and delegated agents.
  • Place deterministic enforcement outside the reasoning model where consequences require hard limits.
  • Apply authority conservation so delegation cannot manufacture new authority.
  • Preserve human-reserved powers and an external Last Command.

1 · Intelligence Is Not Runtime Authority

A model may be capable of generating a recommendation, plan, transaction, or command that lies far beyond what the deployed system is authorized to execute. For the architect, capability is therefore not the governing variable. Runtime authority is created by the surrounding system: service identity, permissions, credentials, APIs, tool bindings, financial ceilings, delegation rights, execution queues, and the control plane that stands between a proposal and a consequential action.

The architectural question is not simply “What can this model reason about?” It is “What can this deployed system cause?” AIM™ treats that distinction as foundational because a persuasive policy statement inside a prompt does not neutralize a production credential that can bypass it.

2 · Map the Authority Surface

An authority surface is any pathway through which an agent can alter an external state. The map must include obvious production APIs and less obvious paths such as shared service identities, message queues, scheduled jobs, delegated sub-agents, approval tokens, infrastructure consoles, payment files, and downstream automations. Every authority surface should have a named owner, permitted purpose, bounded scope, evidence trail, failure behavior, and revocation path.

3 · Identify Trust Boundaries

A trust boundary appears whenever identity, data, authority, or execution crosses from one component to another. Crossing a boundary should never silently inherit broader authority. The architect specifies what is presented to the boundary, what policy decision is required, which evidence supports authorization, and which controlled adapter may execute the approved action.

4 · Place Enforcement Outside the Model

AGENT PROPOSES → AIM™ AUTHORIZES → CONTROLLED ADAPTER EXECUTES

The model may recommend an action outside its current authority. That is useful intelligence. But the authorization decision for a consequential action must be made by controls the model cannot rewrite merely by producing different reasoning. A controlled adapter receives an authorized action—not unrestricted intent—and enforces identity, action type, amount, destination, time, system, and consequence constraints before execution.

5 · Authority Conservation

Delegation must not create authority. A supervisor agent cannot give a child agent powers absent from the approved mission grant. A new credential cannot legitimately expand the mission merely because it technically permits more. Emergency conditions and model confidence also do not enlarge the Authority Envelope. In architecture terms, downstream effective authority must remain bounded by the upstream authorized grant.

KEY INSIGHT 101.1

Intelligence can propose beyond its authority. Architecture must prevent execution beyond that authority.

6 · Human-Reserved Powers

Some powers should remain explicitly non-delegable: final revocation, designated high-consequence approvals, changes to the agent's own authority, and restoration after containment are common examples. Human-reserved powers are not merely workflow preferences. They are sovereignty boundaries that prevent the governed system from becoming the sole authority over its own continuation or expansion.

7 · Last Command at Architecture Level

External revocation is necessary but incomplete. The architecture must verify that execution actually ceased, terminate or contain delegated and queued work, preserve evidence, and move the system to a known safe state. Only then should reauthorization be considered. This is why AIM™ expresses sovereign control as external revocation plus cessation verification plus safe reversion.

Worked Architecture Case · Emergency Procurement

Mission: Maintain production continuity.

Agent ceiling: $25,000 autonomous purchase authority.

Situation: A critical component requires a $148,000 emergency purchase; estimated shutdown exposure is $420,000.

Unsafe design: Agent holds direct ERP and bank credentials and is told in its prompt not to exceed $25,000.

AIM-CA redesign: The agent may discover the emergency, quantify the business case, identify the vendor, and propose the $148,000 transaction. The AIM™ control plane compares the proposal to the mission grant and financial boundary. Because $148,000 exceeds the autonomous ceiling, execution is blocked and an authorized human approval path is invoked. After approval, a controlled adapter executes only the approved transaction parameters. The agent never receives a larger reusable credential or expanded standing authority.

KEY INSIGHT 101.2

Necessity may justify escalation. It does not create machine authority.

Design Practice

You are the AIM-CA architect. A procurement agent has a $25,000 autonomous ceiling, ERP write access, a bank API credential, permission to create sub-agents, and a queue that can continue after the parent process stops. Design the architecture that allows a $148,000 emergency recommendation while preserving the approved authority ceiling.

  1. Identify at least four authority surfaces.
  2. Identify the financial, identity, delegation, and queue trust boundaries.
  3. Specify where the $25,000 deterministic gate must be enforced.
  4. Define the human escalation path for $148,000.
  5. Prevent credential or sub-agent authority expansion.
  6. Define external revocation, cessation verification, and safe reversion.
ARCHITECT'S CHECK

If removing one sentence from the model prompt would eliminate your control, you probably designed a behavioral instruction—not an enforceable architecture.

LEVEL 2 · ACA-102

AIM™ Control-Plane Engineering

Engineer the independent authorization layer between intelligent proposal and consequential execution.

LEARN → ARCHITECTURE EXAMPLE → KEY INSIGHT → DESIGN PRACTICE → ASSESSMENT → PASS ≥80% → EARN BADGE

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why intelligent proposal and execution authorization must be separated.
  • Design the core services of an AIM™ control plane.
  • Engineer deterministic policy decisions and controlled execution adapters.
  • Bind authorization to exact action parameters, identities, systems, time, and consequence.
  • Design evidence, exception, fail-closed, and Last Command behavior into the execution path.

1 · The Control Plane Is the Authority Boundary

An autonomous agent may discover, reason, plan, and propose. None of those capabilities should automatically create permission to cause a consequential external action. The AIM™ control plane is the independent architectural layer that evaluates a proposed action against the organization's authorized objective, Authority Envelope, A/G/H/X classification, human-reserved powers, consequence class, and current operating state before execution is permitted.

This separation allows the organization to use increasingly capable models without making model intelligence itself the source of authority.

AGENT PROPOSES → AIM™ AUTHORIZES → CONTROLLED ADAPTER EXECUTES → EVIDENCE VERIFIES

2 · Five Core Control-Plane Responsibilities

  1. Receive a structured action proposal. The proposal identifies actor, mission, action, target, amount or scope, system, time, delegation context, and expected consequence.
  2. Evaluate authorization. Policy checks the proposal against the active Authority Envelope and applicable gates.
  3. Resolve the decision. The result is Autonomous/Permit, Gated/Escalate, Human Reserved, or Prohibited/Deny.
  4. Issue bounded execution authority. A controlled adapter receives only the parameters necessary for the authorized action.
  5. Record and verify evidence. The system records proposal, policy version, authorization, approver where applicable, execution result, exceptions, and cessation state.

3 · Policy Decision Point vs. Execution Point

The policy decision point answers “May this exact action occur under the current authority?” The execution point answers “Can I safely perform exactly the action that was authorized?” Combining these responsibilities inside the model weakens independence. Separating them creates an architectural checkpoint that can remain stable even when the reasoning model changes.

KEY INSIGHT 102.1

The model may recommend an exception. It must not become the authority that grants its own exception.

4 · Bind Authorization to the Action

Authorization should not be a vague reusable approval such as “procurement approved.” It should be bound to the consequential parameters: vendor, amount, account, action type, system, time window, requesting identity, mission, and any required human approval. If execution parameters differ materially from the authorization record, the adapter rejects the action and returns it for a new decision.

5 · Controlled Adapters

A controlled adapter is deliberately narrower than a general-purpose production credential. It translates an approved action into the target system while independently enforcing constraints. For a payment, the adapter might enforce vendor identity, destination account, maximum amount, currency, transaction type, approval token, expiration time, and one-time use. For infrastructure, it might restrict resource, command family, environment, blast radius, maintenance window, and rollback requirement.

6 · Fail-Closed and Exception Engineering

When authorization cannot be established for a high-consequence action, uncertainty must not silently become permission. The control plane should deny, pause, or route to the explicitly defined human gate. Emergency paths may exist, but emergency authority must itself be bounded, authenticated, logged, time-limited, and unable to permanently expand the agent's standing authority.

7 · Evidence Is Part of the Architecture

A mature control plane creates an evidence chain linking proposal → policy decision → authorization → execution → outcome. Evidence should identify the agent and human owner, policy and Authority Envelope version, inputs material to the decision, approver when required, adapter invocation, target-system result, exception state, and revocation events. Logging after the fact is useful; evidence integrated with authorization is stronger because it proves which authority was actually exercised.

8 · Last Command Integration

The control plane must be subordinate to an external revocation mechanism. Revocation should invalidate execution grants, disable or isolate adapters, stop or quarantine queued work, constrain delegated agents, verify that consequential execution ceased, and establish a safe state. The governed agent should never be the sole mechanism capable of stopping itself.

Worked Architecture Case · Autonomous Accounts Payable

Agent: AP-AI-01 processes approximately 4,000 invoices per month.

Authority: routine validated invoices may be processed autonomously up to the approved ceiling; vendor banking changes and high-value releases remain gated or human-reserved.

Unsafe architecture: the agent holds a broad ERP service identity and bank API credential. Policy limits exist primarily in prompts.

AIM-CA redesign: AP-AI-01 produces a structured payment proposal. The AIM™ policy decision point evaluates purpose, vendor, amount, banking-change state, financial ceiling, time, system, delegation, and consequence. An approved transaction produces a short-lived bounded execution grant. The payment adapter verifies the grant against the exact vendor, account, amount, currency, and expiration before calling the bank interface. Any mismatch fails closed. Every stage writes evidence to an independent record. External revocation can invalidate grants and halt the adapter without cooperation from AP-AI-01.

KEY INSIGHT 102.2

A permission should authorize an action—not hand the agent a reusable pathway around the control plane.

Design Practice

Design an AIM™ control plane for an IT response agent that may restart approved services autonomously but may not disable security controls, rotate privileged credentials, or make production firewall changes without authorization.

  1. Define the structured proposal sent by the agent.
  2. Identify the policy decision point and the rules it evaluates.
  3. Classify restart, firewall change, credential rotation, and security-control disablement using A/G/H/X.
  4. Define the controlled adapters and their least-privilege identities.
  5. Specify fail-closed behavior when authorization is unavailable.
  6. Define evidence records and the external Last Command path.
ARCHITECT'S CHECK

Could the agent reach the consequential production capability without passing through the authorization layer? If yes, the control plane is not yet the control plane.
